summary: A sequence of steps with per-step validation, where progress survives leaving.
useWhen: a task genuinely has an order — later steps depend on earlier answers
the whole task is too long to present as one form without abandonment
structure: A step indicator naming every step and marking the current one — not Tabs, because the steps are not peers and cannot be visited in any order.
One step's fields at a time, each step a Form in its own right.
Back and Next, plus save-and-exit for anything longer than three steps.
A final review step listing every answer with a link back to the step that set it.

loading.must: Disable Next and say what is happening on it. Never advance optimistically.
loading.why: advancing before the server accepts step N means step N+1 may be built on rejected data

empty.must: A resumed wizard opens on the first incomplete step, not step one.
empty.why: restarting a half-finished task is why users abandon it the second time

error.must: Stay on the failing step, mark the fields, and keep every answer from every step.
error.why: losing step 1's answers because step 3 failed is the worst version of this pattern

partial.must: Save each completed step as it is accepted, so leaving mid-wizard loses at most the current step.
partial.why: save-and-exit that only saves at the end is not save-and-exit

requires: the step change announced, and focus moved to the new step's heading — otherwise a screen-reader user does not know the page changed
the current step's position stated in text, not only drawn: "Step 2 of 5"
each step's fields validated on its own Next, not all at the end
notes: Do not build this from Tabs. The tablist role announces peers that may be visited in any order, which is the opposite of a wizard.
A Modal wraps the whole wizard only when abandoning it is safe. A long task in a dialog that closes on an outside click loses everything.

antiPatterns.why: the role promises peers in any order, and nothing stops a user landing on the last step first

antiPatterns.dont: validating every step only at the end
antiPatterns.why: the user is sent back through steps they thought were finished

antiPatterns.dont: a wizard for a task that fits on one screen
antiPatterns.why: each step boundary is an opportunity to abandon

antiPatterns.dont: a progress bar with no step names
antiPatterns.why: a percentage does not tell the user what is left or whether they can finish now
